```{r table-styling}
ellipsis <- function(df, nhead=5L, ntail=2) {
    rownames(df) = as.character(1:nrow(df))
    stopifnot("data.frame" %in% class(df))
    els <- rep(NA, ncol(df)) %>% 
        matrix(nrow=1, dimnames=list(NULL, names(df))) %>% 
        data.frame(stringsAsFactors=FALSE) %>% 
        tibble::as_tibble()
    rownames(els) = "⋮"
    dplyr::bind_rows(head(df, nhead), els, tail(df, ntail))
}
```

```{r transform-data}
#| cache: false
#| 
all.earnings = data.frame(state.code = cps.data$gestfips,
                          county.code = cps.data$gtco,
                          year=cps.data$year,
                          age=cps.data$a_age,
                          income=cps.data$pearnval,
                          education.code=cps.data$a_hga,
                          education=case_match(cps.data$a_hga,
                                           0  ~ 0,   # child
                                           31 ~ 0,   # < grade 1
                                           32 ~ 4,   #  grade 1-4
                                           33 ~ 6,   #  grade 5-6
                                           34 ~ 8,   #  grade 7-8 
                                           35 ~ 9,   #  grade 9
                                           36 ~ 10,  #  grade 10
                                           37 ~ 11,  #  grade 11
                                           38 ~ 11,  #  grade 12 no diploma
                                           39 ~ 12,  #  high school grad
                                           40 ~ 13,  #  some college
                                           41 ~ 14,  #  associate degree (vocational)
                                           42 ~ 14,  #  associate degree (academic)
                                           43 ~ 16,  #  bachelors degree
                                           44 ~ 18,  #  masters degree
                                           45 ~ 20,  #  professional school degree
                                           46 ~ 20)) #  doctorate

all.earnings$degree = factor(all.earnings$education >= 16, 
                     levels=c(FALSE, TRUE), 
                     labels=c('no 4-year degree','4-year degree')) 

coarsen = function(x, group, seed=0) {
  current.seed = .Random.seed
  set.seed(seed)
  x.coarsened = rep(NA, length(x))
  for(gg in unique(group)) {
    x.coarsened[group==gg] = runif(sum(group==gg), min(x[group==gg]), max(x[group==gg]))
  }
  set.seed(current.seed)
  x.coarsened
} 
```

```{r}
paradox = purrr::map(unique(all.earnings$state.code), function(code) {
  in.interval = function(X, interval) { interval[1] <= X & X <= interval[2] }
  earnings = filter(all.earnings, education >= 8 & 
                                state.code == code)
  aggregate.model = lm(income ~ year, data=earnings)
  group.model = lm(income ~ year + degree, data=earnings)
  data.frame(code=code, happens=coef(aggregate.model)[2] * coef(group.model)[2] < 0) 
}) %>% bind_rows()

codes=unique(paradox$code[paradox$happens])
```

## Simpson's Paradox {.smaller}

::: {.center}
![](figures/finalAct2){height=400px}
:::

- Sometimes, the *aggregate relationship* between two variables is opposite the *within-groups relationship*.
- Above, the aggregate relationship is positive. But the within-groups relationship is negative.
- We can see this when we compare the slopes $\hat\beta_1$ we get by fitting two models.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x } \qquad        & \text{univariate model} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z} \qquad & \text{additive bivariate model}
\end{aligned}
}
$$

- We didn't really need to fit a regression model to see this. It's obvious from the scatterplot.
- Sometimes things are a bit less obvious and we need to fit a model to see it. 

## Pandemic-Era Income Growth in Manhattan 

```{r}
#| out-height: 400px
 
in_interval = function(X, interval) { interval[1] <= X & X <= interval[2] }
earnings = all.earnings %>% filter(education >= 8 & state.code==36 & county.code==61)
aggregate.model = lm(income ~ year, data=earnings)
group.model = lm(income ~ year + degree, data=earnings)

summaries = earnings %>% group_by(year) %>% summarize(mean=mean(income), sd=sd(income), n=n())
group.summaries = earnings %>% group_by(year, degree) %>% summarize(mean=mean(income), sd=sd(income), n=n())
grid = expand.grid(year=unique(earnings$year), degree=unique(earnings$degree))
grid$aggregate = predict(aggregate.model, newdata=grid)
grid$group = predict(group.model, newdata=grid)

ggplot(earnings) + geom_point(aes(x=year, y=income, color=degree), alpha=.2, size=.5, position=position_jitter(width=.1)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(x=year, y=mean, ymin=mean-sd/sqrt(n), ymax=mean+sd/sqrt(n)), data=summaries) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(x=year+.1*(2*(degree=='4-year degree')-1), y=mean, ymin=mean-sd/sqrt(n), ymax=mean+sd/sqrt(n), color=degree), data=group.summaries) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=dollar_format(), limits=c(0, 200000)) +
  geom_line(aes(x=year, y=aggregate), data=grid, linetype='dashed') +
  geom_line(aes(x=year, y=group, color=degree), data=grid, linetype='dashed') 
```

- Above, we're looking at income growth, i.e. the relationship between year and income.
- We're looking at it for Manhattan residents who responded to the CPS.
- In aggregate, income growth is negative. But within groups, income growth is positive.
- **Q**. What's going on? Think about the time period we're looking at.

\ \

::: fragment

- People with 4-year degrees, who tend to have higher incomes, moved away during the pandemic.
- You can see this by looking at the fraction of respondents with 4-year degrees over time.

:::


## Omitted Variable Bias
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&\qfor \hat\beta = \argmin_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_i - Y_i }^2
\end{aligned}
$$

- We can understand what we're seeing as a form of **omitted variable bias**.
- Omitted variable bias is the **change in a slope parameter** when we **omit a covariate** from our model.
- The formula above is a special case. 
- It's the slope in the **univariate model** that we get by omitting $Z$ from the **additive model**.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x } \qquad        & \text{univariate model} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z} \qquad & \text{additive bivariate model}
\end{aligned}
$$

## OVB and Covariate Balance


$$
\small{
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\textcolor{blue}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2}
}
$$

- Leaving $Z$ out doesn't result in OVB when $X$ and $Z$ are *uncorrelated*.
- When $X$ is binary, this happens when $Z$ has the same mean in two subsamples.
- The subsample where $X=1$ and the whole sample.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\textcolor{blue}{\sum_i (X_i - \bar X) Z_i} 
= \sum_i X_i Z_i - \bar X \sum_i Z_i  
&= \sum_i X_i \times \frac{\sum_i X_i Z_i}{\sum_i X_i} - \frac{\sum_i X_i}{n} \times \sum_i Z_i  \\
&= \sum_i X_i \times \qty( \frac{\sum_i X_i Z_i}{\sum_i X_i} - \frac{\sum_i Z_i}{n} ) 
\end{aligned}
}
$$

- Or, equivalently, when its mean is the same in the $X=0$ and $X=1$ subsamples. 
- That's what we see in *balance tables*. 

## An Example

![](figures/GGL.png){height=400px}

- Suppose we're comparing Civic Duty and Control.
$$
X_i = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{ if person $i$ receives Civic Duty} \\
0 & \text{ if person $i$ receives Control}
\end{cases}
$$

- We want to see our covariate means are zero in the subsamples receiving those two treatments.
- That tells us it doesn't matter whether we include any one covariate $Z$. We're not going to get OVB.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(X_i - \bar X) Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat \beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \sum_i X_i \times \qty( \frac{\sum_i X_i Z_i}{\sum_i X_i} - \frac{\sum_i Z_i}{n} )  
\end{aligned}
}
$$

## Thinking About Our Example More Carefully

![](figures/GGL.png){height=400px}

- But we're not really talking about leaving out any one covariate $Z$. 
- We're talking about leaving out *all 8* in the table above.
- That, roughly speaking, is the difference between the models that were considered in this study.
- The good news is that our formula generalizes. We can leave out *any number of balanced covariates* without OVB.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat \beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i1}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
+\hat \beta_3 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i2}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} + \ldots \\
&\qfor \hat\beta = \argmin_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_{i1} + b_3 Z_{i2} + \ldots - Y_i}^2
\end{aligned}
}
$$

##  Could **Covariate Interaction Terms** Change Things?

![](figures/GGL.png){height=400px}


- We do have OVB formulas telling us it won't *if the interaction is balanced*.
- Here's one for leaving out two *interacted covariates*. And it generalizes to any number.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i1}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&+ \hat\beta_3 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i2}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} +
 + \hat\beta_4 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i1} Z_{i2} Z_{i2}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&\qfor \hat\beta = \argmin_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_{i1} + b_3 Z_{i2} + b_4 Z_{i1} Z_{i2} - Y_i}^2
\end{aligned}
}
$$

:::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="0"}

- **Q.** What's missing?

:::
::: {.fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}

- **Q.** What's missing? **A.** The information to use it. Our table doesn't show balance in any interactions. 

:::
::::

## What About **Treatment/Covariate Interactions**?

- You could try to make the same argument---that we don't have the information---but it doesn't work.
- We do have the information. We just have to be a bit clever with our arithmetic.
- Here's the **slope of a univariate model** in terms of the coefficients of a **bivariate model** with treatment/covariate interaction.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
+ \hat\beta_3 \textcolor{blue}{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) X_i Z_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2}} \\
&\qfor \hat\beta = \argmin_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_{i} + b_3 X_i Z_{i} - Y_i}^2
\end{aligned}
}
$$

- And we can calculate this [new factor]{.fg style="text:blue"} using information we have.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\textcolor{blue}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) X_i Z_i}
&= \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 Z_{i} - \bar X \sum_{i=1}^n X_i Z_{i} = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i Z_{i}   - \bar X \sum_{i=1}^n X_i Z_{i} \\
&= (1-\bar X)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i Z_i = (1-\bar X)\bar X \times n \times \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}
\end{aligned}
}
$$

- But we see that the slope coefficients $\hat\beta_1$ in these two models are essentially never the same. 
- This formula doesn't require *agreement* between subsample means. It requires them to be zero.

## Is This A Bad Thing?

:::: columns
::: column
![](figures/finalAct3){height=400px}
:::
::: column
Hint. Think about *predictions*, not *coefficients*.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\hat \mu(x+1,z)-\hat\mu(x,z)   &= \hat\beta_1 && \text{ in the univariate model } \\ 
\hat \mu(x+1,z)-\hat\mu(x,z)   &= \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3 z && \text{ in the interacted model } 
\end{aligned}
}
$$
:::
::::

:::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="0"}
- No, not really. It doesn't really make sense to compare these two slope coefficients.
- The slope coefficients $\hat\beta_1$ in these two models do not mean the same thing.
- It's more reasonable to compare the *average slope* in the interacted model to *the slope* in the univariate model.
:::
::: {.fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}
- And the average slope in the interacted model isn't $\hat\beta_1$. It's between the $z=0$ and $z=1$ slopes. 
- For $z \in [0,1]$, that's between $\hat \beta_1$ and $\hat\beta_1+\hat \beta_3$.
- **Takeaway.** We need the coefficients $\hat\beta_1$ to be different for the average slopes to be the same.
:::
::::


## Why are we talking about OVB formulas? 

- These formulas compare **estimated coefficients** in two models. 
    - At best, it's the difference between two estimators of the same thing.
    - At worst, it's something else entirely.
- In any case, that's not what bias is. 
    - Bias isn't about the relationship between two estimators.
    - It's about the relationship between an estimator and what it's meant to estimate.
- We've been talking about OVB because it's a good warm-up for the real thing. 
- We'll get there, but we're going to take a bit of a detour we're going to take first.
    - We've been talking about a few simple *bivariate models*. 
    - Now we're going to talk about regression models in general.
- This should, in the end, make it easier to understand what bias really is.

## One Thing To Notice

- All of our OVB formulas are essentially the same.
- All we need to do is think of interaction terms as *additional covariates* in an additive model.
    - If we take $Z_4=Z_1 Z_2$ in our first formula, we get the second---a formula for interacted covariates.
    - If we take $Z_2=X Z$ in our first formula, we get the third---a formula for treatment/covariate interactions.

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat \beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i1}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
+\hat \beta_3 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i2}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} + \ldots \\
&\color{gray} \qfor \hat\beta = \argmin_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_{i1} + b_3 Z_{i2} + \ldots - Y_i}^2 \\
&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i1}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&+ \hat\beta_3 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i2}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} +
 + \hat\beta_4 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i1} Z_{i2} Z_{i2}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&\color{gray}\qfor \hat\beta = \argmin_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_{i1} + b_3 Z_{i2} + b_4 Z_{i1} Z_{i2} - Y_i}^2 \\
&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
+ \hat\beta_3 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) X_i Z_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&\color{gray} \qfor \hat\beta = \argmin_{b} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_{i} + b_3 X_i Z_{i} - Y_i}^2
\end{aligned}
}
$$

- This is a general phenomenon in linear regression. The math for additive models ... 
- also works for additive models in *functions* of the covariates---like interactions.
- In the Machine Learning tradition, we tend to call these functions *features*.

# Regression in General

## What Regression Is

$$ Y_i \approx \hat\mu(X_i) \qfor \hat\mu \in \model \qqtext{where} \hat \mu = \argmin_{m \in \model} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ m(\textbf{X}_i) - Y_i}^2 $$

- Regression is **choosing a function** of covariates $\textbf{X}_i$ to predict outcomes $Y_i$.
- Typically---and we'll follow this convention---we'll think of $Y_i$ as a real number.
- But $\textbf{X}_i$ can be anything. 
    - A real number---univariate regression: $\textbf{X}_i = X_i$
    - Two real numbers $\textbf{X}_i=(X_i,Z_i)$.
    - K real numbers $\textbf{X}_i=(X_{i1},X_{i2},...,X_{iK})$.
    - An image, a text document, a function, etc.
- And what sort of thing it is doesn't really change how it works mathematically.
    - The reason is that the math doesn't really look at the covariate $X$. 
    - It only looks at the values $m(\textbf{X}_i)$ of the functions we're considering. 
- Linear regression is a special case in which we choose $m$ from a **linear model**.
- That is, a set of functions we can combine by adding and scaling without leaving the model.

$$ \small{ m_1, m_2 \in \model \implies b_1 m_1 + b_2 m_2 \in \model \qqtext{ for all } b_1,b_2 \in \R }$$


## Linear Models {.smaller}

```{r}
#| out-height: 600px
 
ggplot(earnings) + geom_point(aes(x=year, y=income, color=degree), alpha=.2, size=.5, position=position_jitter(width=.1)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(x=year+.1*(2*(degree=='4-year degree')-1), y=mean, ymin=mean-sd/sqrt(n), ymax=mean+sd/sqrt(n), color=degree), data=group.summaries) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=dollar_format(), limits=c(0, 200000)) 
```



- The first linear model we worked with was **the saturated model**. 
    - We call it *saturated* because it *every function of $x$*---to make $m(x_j)=y$, set $b_j=y$. 
    - This model couldn't be misspecified. 
    - No matter what the true relationship between $X$ and $Y$ was, it was in the model.
    - When we fit it via least squares, our prediction $\hat\mu(x)$ was the mean of $Y_i$ on the subsample with $X_i=x$ 
$$
\small{
\model = \qty{ m(x) = \sum_j b_j 1_{x_j}(x) : b_j \in \R } 
}
$$    

## More Linear Models {.smaller}

![](figures/finalAct1){height=600px}

- The second linear model we worked with was the set of **lines**.
    - When $x$ is binary, this was just a different way of writing the saturated model. - There's a line through any two points $(0,m(0))$ and $(1,m(1))$.
    - But with many-valued $x$, we started having to worry about **misspecification**.
    - To reduce misspecification, people often use higher-order **polynomials** instead.
$$\small{
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = b_0 + b_1 x : b_0,b_1 \in \R } && \text{lines} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2: b_0,b_1,b_2 \in \R } && \text{quadratic polynomials}
\end{aligned}
}
$$

## Bivariate Models {.smaller}

![](figures/finalAct3){height=600px}

- In the last two classes, we've talked about two *bivariate models*.

$$\small{
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x_1,x_2) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2 x_2 : b \in \R^3 }                 &&\text{additive bivariate model} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x_1,x_2) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_1 x_2: b \in \R^4 }      &&\text{interacted bivariate model} \\
\end{aligned}
}
$$


## What Do All Of These Models Have in Common?

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = \sum_j b_j 1_{x_j}(x) : b_j \in \R } && \text{saturated} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = b_0 + b_1 x : b_0,b_1 \in \R } && \text{lines} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2: b_0,b_1,b_2 \in \R } && \text{quadratic polynomials} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x_1,x_2) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2 x_2 : b \in \R^3 }                 &&\text{additive bivariate model} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x_1,x_2) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_1 x_2: b \in \R^4 }      &&\text{interacted bivariate model} \\
\end{aligned}
}
$$

::: fragment

- They're the set of **all linear combinations** of a set of **features**.
$$
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = \sum_j b_j \phi_j(x) : b \in \R^{K+1} } && \text{ general form }
\end{aligned}
$$

- If you know the features $\phi_j$, you know the model---the set of curves $m(x)$.
- And if you know the model---the set of curves---you can work out a corresponding set of features. 
- That's a matter of linear algebra. We'll look into that in a few weeks.




:::

## Exercise: List the Features $\phi_j$ for Each Model

$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = \sum_j b_j 1_{x_j}(x) : b_j \in \R } && \text{saturated} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = b_0 + b_1 x : b_0,b_1 \in \R } && \text{lines} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2: b_0,b_1,b_2 \in \R } && \text{quadratic polynomials} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x_1,x_2) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2 x_2 : b \in \R^3 }                 &&\text{additive bivariate model} \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x_1,x_2) = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_1 x_2: b \in \R^4 }      &&\text{interacted bivariate model} \\
\end{aligned}
}
$$


## Least Squares in General

### Choosing a Curve --- Useful for Thinking

$$
\hat \mu = \argmin_{m \in \model} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ m(\textbf{X}_i) - Y_i}^2 \qqtext{ for } \model = \qty{ m(x) = \sum_j b_j \phi_j(x) : b \in \R^{K+1} }
$$

### Finding Coefficients --- Useful for Math

$$
\hat \mu(x) = \sum_{0=1}^K \hat\beta_j \phi_j(x) \qqtext{ where } \hat\beta = \argmin_{b \in \R^{K+1}} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ \sum_j b_j \phi_j(\textbf{X}_i) - Y_i}^2
$$

## Least Squares Residuals

[TODO: 4 PLOT]

The residuals $\hat\varepsilon_i = Y_i - \hat\mu(X_i)$ are **orthogonal** to the every feature $\phi_j(X_i)$.
$$
\small{
\sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i \phi_j(X_i) = 0 \qfor j=0,1,\ldots,K
}
$$

Familiar example ...

## Least Squares Residuals

This means they're **orthogonal** to every curve $m(x)$ in the model.
$$
\small{
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n  \hat\varepsilon_i m(X_i) 
&=  \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i \qty{ \sum_j b_j \phi_j(X_i) } && \text{ for any $m \in \model$ } \\
&=  \sum_j \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i b_j \phi_j(X_i)         && \text{ distributing } \\
&=  \sum_j b_j \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i \phi_j(X_i)         && \text{ pulling out constants} \\
&=  \sum_j b_j \times 0 = 0                              
\end{aligned}
}
$$

## Least Squares Residuals

*If the constant $1$ is in the model*, this means they're **uncorrelated** with every curve in the model. Why?

::: fragment

$$
m \in \model \qqtext{ and } 1 \in \model \implies m - \bar m \times 1 \in \model \qqtext{ for the `coefficient' } \bar m = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n m(X_i)
$$

and therefore

$$
\sum_i \hat\varepsilon_i \qty{ m(X_i) - \bar m } = 0 \qfor m \in \model
$$

:::

## Proof

$$
\small{
\qqtext{Let's prove that } \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i \phi_j(X_i) = 0 \qfor j=0,1,\ldots,K
}
$$
